item.text: Level 1 reliably reaches the level-2 entry in 13 moves. I’m now creating a minimal observational probe that enters level 2 through the known leg, then compares cloned one-step action effects and compact component summaries—no game internals or prior transcripts.

The clone deltas identify the avatar as a persistent 5×5 two-color object: action 1 moves it up and action 4 right; actions 2 and 3 are presently blocked. A separate bottom strip shrinks by four cells every turn, so I’m treating it as a move budget, not progress. The dense state I’ll search is avatar position/orientation plus remaining small color-11 objects, which avoids branching on the countdown animation.

The first bounded search falsifies “simply walk to either visible marker” within 30 steps. I’m narrowing the mechanic next: the avatar’s two-color footprint moves as one rigid piece, but downward motion is blocked despite no obvious target contact. I’ll inspect only compact non-background row runs around the playfield and test short reversals to distinguish collision from direction/state constraints.

The collision explanation is now verified: color 4 forms a 5-pixel maze. The start has walls immediately left and below, so only up/right are legal there. A static route reaches the upper color-11 marker in 12 moves; I’m testing that subgoal directly and measuring whether the marker disappears, transforms, or raises reward before planning beyond it.

Both color-11 markers are collectible and the planned route removes both, but reward stays flat, so “collect all markers” is only a subgoal. The remaining distinctive reachable object is a tiny color-0/1 symbol in the lower-right corridor; I’m testing it as the exit unlocked by those collectibles.

No reachable position completes the level after the two collectibles, so the lower-right symbol is not a conventional exit. The shrinking strip is now the leading candidate for a stateful completion condition; I’ll measure it after the collectible route and advance time using blocked moves to see whether collection must be followed by a countdown phase.

The strip behavior is now verified: it resets to full whenever a marker is collected, and exhausting it resets the level while consuming one color-8 life. That gives a precise dense measure and implies route segments must each be ≤21 moves. I found a better order: lower marker in 20 moves, then upper in 18, each safely refreshing the timer. I’m testing that order before adding any return leg.

Returning to the start is not the terminal condition. The tiny color-0/1 object has the visual structure and location of a checkered finish, but merely overlapping it did not immediately reward. I’m testing whether it is a timed finish/checkpoint and whether the symbol itself changes on contact; this also checks the countdown-dependent state that the position-only BFS intentionally pruned.

Contact removes the checkered symbol but does not refill the timer, so it is a third required pickup rather than a finish. A feasible schedule exists: reach the checkered pickup in 16 moves, reach the lower timer marker three moves later (refresh), then the upper marker in 18 (refresh). I’m testing that complete three-object route and checking whether it unlocks the embedded left-side door.

The checkered object reappears after the avatar leaves, so it is only being visually occluded—not collected. I’m broadening the verified symbolic search to 80 moves while keying on avatar position and remaining real collectibles. Because collecting a marker changes that key and refreshes the timer, this preserves meaningful progress without exploding on animation frames.

The broad position/collectible search finds no generic “stand here” win, so entry direction or contact context matters. I’m now testing the checkered cell from all four approach directions after both timer markers are collected; this is the smallest falsifiable context experiment before introducing countdown state into search.

All four entry directions to the checkered cell are non-terminal, so it is not a directional exit. One remaining ambiguity is the bottom system: the three color-8 blocks behave like lives, but I’ll verify whether exhausting them is failure or an unusual completion condition before searching timer-phase state.

Exhausting the color-8 blocks is confirmed failure, and the checkered cell alone is not the goal. I’m taking one compact visual inspection of the raw level now to classify the remaining small sprites by shape; all movement and state conclusions will still be verified through clone actions.

The visual resolves the remaining object classes: the gray/maroon patterned block in the left cul-de-sac is paired with a larger gray/maroon reference icon in the UI, while the black/blue sprite is separate. The patterned block is the strongest goal/mechanic candidate. I’ll probe a collision with it both before and after collecting both timer rings, comparing only that object’s pixels and reward.

The patterned block is not solid: moving down from the cul-de-sac enters it and overwrites its top edge. That is a new mechanic the coarse maze abstraction hid. I’m testing successive passes through the block and then moving away to determine whether the avatar paints/erases it persistently and whether matching the UI reference is the actual win condition.
